content.thinking:
I need to avoid citing figures directly and instead explain what they meant for actual users—the series shown isn't error rate but memory usage, which climbing toward its limit would risk account page failures or latency rather than directly showing failed requests. I should frame this as heap warnings rising and real impact on account page errors, not just restate that nothing failed.

For the causal chain, I'm laying out the steps carefully: memory rose steadily while error rate held flat, heap climbed toward its configured limit, no deployments or config changes occurred during the window, and traffic stayed level—though I need to be careful since that flat-traffic claim only appears in the candidate's version, not in cited evidence, so I should leave it out. The key confirmed finding is that memory wasn't released by the process itself and only returned to baseline after a restart.

Root cause: an unreleased heap growth in the io-shop process, with the underlying code defect never identified in the record, though a fix has been drafted in a pull request still awaiting review.

For contributing factors, I'm noting that the alert was named for high memory but its description text referenced an error-rate threshold instead—a mismatch worth flagging. I also want to calculate the detection delay between when heap warnings began at 12:16 and when the alert actually fired at 12:26:47, since that gap suggests detection came too late relative to onset. This points to needing new action items: fixing the mismatched alert text, adding earlier heap-growth-trend alerting, and tracking the leak fix itself—numbered sequentially as AI-2 through AI-4. I'm also double-checking that account page error rates in the reference data look normal, and noting that a 48-hour claim from the candidate source isn't something I can verify yet.

On the positive side, the restart is confirmed to have worked, and the system got lucky—heap peaked at 1326 MiB against the 2048 MiB limit, so it never actually hit an out-of-memory condition before the restart intervened. There's a subtle timing discrepancy though: metrics show recovery starting right around 12:27, but the restart itself wasn't issued until slightly after that mark, so I shouldn't assume the restart was definitively the sole cause of recovery—I'll flag this as an assumption rather than a certainty, while still noting the system was back at baseline by 12:27.

action_items.item: Correct the HighMemoryUsage alert description so it reports memory use and the heap limit, not an error rate.
Add an early-warning alert on sustained heap growth toward the limit, so that it fires before the paging threshold and before memory is exhausted.

causal_chain.step: Memory use on io-shop rose from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average and {series_at_worst} at its worst, which paged HighMemoryUsage. The error rate did not rise ({errors_while_broken} against {errors_before} before), so shoppers were not failing more often. The service was heading toward its memory ceiling.
The process heap grew steadily, from {G9c6f.5} to {G9c6f.6} against a {G9c6f.1} limit, with the highest reading at {G9c6f.8}. It did not settle back to its usual {G9c6f.7}.
Nothing external explains the growth. No production change and no flag change was found in the windows read.
Memory was not being released inside the running process. Restarting io-shop returned the service to its baseline and the paging rule stopped firing.
The code path that holds the memory is not identified in the record. A draft fix was proposed as a pull request and is still unmerged, so the evidence stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The restart only clears the symptom. The underlying memory growth is still in the code until the proposed fix is reviewed and merged, so it can recur.
Heap warnings began well before the page. The alert came at {alert_raised}, which is {alert_raised - began} after onset. Nothing watched the heap growth trend or the nearness to the limit.
The alert is named HighMemoryUsage but its text says 'Error rate above threshold', although no more requests failed. This misdescribes the problem to whoever is paged.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, memory use on the shop service climbed well above normal. The series that paged rose from {series_before} to {series_at_worst} at its worst. The share of failed requests did not rise: it was {errors_while_broken} against {errors_before} before. Shoppers did not see more errors, but the service was heading toward its memory limit. Had it reached the limit, account pages could have failed or slowed. The automated response restarted the service. Memory returned to its baseline, and the alert stopped firing. A draft fix has been proposed, but until it is merged the same growth can come back.

got_lucky: The heap peaked below its limit, so the process did not run out of memory and no account pages failed.
The metrics already showed recovery at {recovered}, so the service may have been steadying on its own around the time of the restart.
went_well: Argus took the alert up within seconds. It checked changes, flags, logs and metrics, and found no external trigger.
The restart was confirmed against the metrics, and a draft fix was proposed straight away.
went_wrong: The alert text described an error rate, not memory, which is misleading.
Heap warnings were already in the logs well before the alert fired, but nothing acted on them.
The root defect is still unfixed and the fix is only a draft.

input.root_cause: The io-shop process's memory kept growing and was not released, so heap use climbed toward its limit. No deploy, release or flag change preceded it. The record does not show which code path holds the memory. A proposed fix is in draft (AI-2) and has not been merged.
input.symptom: Shop memory climbed toward its limit
